Based on his article on the AdSense situation, Ralph now agrees with you, but I do not. Basically, I think there's a fundamental difference between punishing major Establishment outlets that are either outright corrupt, Censoring discussion or attacking their core readership with email campaigns, and running email campaigns against an independent blogger because he put something "Offensive" up on his site.

I have no sympathy for Gawker for anything that happened to them, and I take pleasure in seeing them struggling even if I don't agree with the tactics used, but I think it's a better strategy to shed light on how corrupt they are (which was definitely happening in addition to the email campaigns). Trying to punish them or take them down doesn't really accomplish anything, because if Gawker goes under there will be another site filling their market the next day. Buzzfeed and Polygon suddenly get far more clicks. We know this first hand; when GG was banned on 4chan, aGG was real smug about it, but 4chan's GG just went to 8chan and were just as strong as ever. It's like playing whack-a-mole. It might feel good to take them down a peg, but you can only take down what they represent by showing people why they are bad. Gawker is just the face of a much deeper problem that must be attacked at the root.

Gawker is the establishment not because they inherited that position undeservedly, but because people continue to read them and support them and enjoy their content, and they give those people what they want. It's their readers holding them up. The day when everyone knows why clickbait is bad is the day clickbait disappears. There's plenty of arguments to be made about whether it's justified going after advertisers or not, but I think educating people and exposing wrongdoings is a much better tactic anyway.
